question: A 9-year-old boy is referred because his teacher reports poor attention, frequent seat-leaving, and disruptive behaviour in class. His parents say he is 'perfectly fine' at home and have never noticed similar behaviour there. Neuropsychological testing shows an IQ of 102. Which statement BEST applies DSM-5 criteria for an ADHD diagnosis in this child?

answers.text: ADHD can be diagnosed because the school symptoms are severe, well-documented by the teacher, and have persisted for over 6 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. DSM-5 requires that symptoms be present in TWO OR MORE settings (e.g., home and school). Symptoms reported only at school, with no corroborating evidence at home, do not fulfil the multi-setting criterion. The diagnosis cannot be made on school-only reports alone.

answers.text: The multi-setting criterion is not met; ADHD diagnosis requires impairment documented in two or more settings, so additional history from the home environment is needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DSM-5 requires that several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are present in two or more settings AND cause impairment in both. With parents reporting no problems at home, the multi-setting criterion is unmet. Further structured home observation or use of validated parent rating scales (e.g., Conners', Vanderbilt) is required before a diagnosis can be made.

answers.text: ADHD is excluded because the child has normal intelligence — ADHD only occurs in children with intellectual disability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ADHD occurs across the full intelligence range, including children with normal and above-normal IQ. DSM-5 does not require intellectual disability for ADHD; the diagnosis is based on symptom profile, onset, duration, multi-setting impairment, and exclusion of other conditions.

answers.text: ADHD diagnosis requires an EEG or brain MRI to confirm — clinical assessment alone is insufficient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ADHD is a CLINICAL diagnosis. There is no EEG pattern, brain scan finding, or blood test that confirms ADHD. DSM-5 criteria are based on history, direct observation, validated rating scales, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Neuroimaging is not part of the standard diagnostic work-up.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key DSM-5 point: ADHD requires symptoms in TWO OR MORE settings (e.g., home AND school), onset before age 12, duration ≥6 months, and impairment in ≥2 settings. It is a clinical diagnosis — no EEG or brain imaging is required.

Well done. DSM-5 ADHD diagnosis requires symptoms in two or more settings. Single-setting reports alone are insufficient — parent-completed rating scales and structured home observation are needed to complete the assessment.
